title: Stacks and queues

outcomes.can: Predict the order in which a stack and a queue give items back.
Use a stack to match each item with the most recent unmatched one.
Build a queue whose operations each take one step.

intro: Some problems only ever need the newest item, and some only the oldest. A stack and a queue are arrays used with that one restriction. The restriction is the point: it makes the code simpler, and it makes every operation take one step. This module covers both, and the trap in building a queue on an array.

steps.title: Last in, first out
steps.text:
A **stack** gives back the item that was added most recently. Think of a pile of plates: you add to the top and take from the top. The two operations are **push**, which adds, and **pop**, which removes and returns the newest.

An array is a ready-made stack. `push` and `pop` both work at the end, so each takes one step.

A stack fits any problem where the thing you need next is the most recent thing you have not dealt with yet: matching brackets, undo, working out an expression, and following a path that you may need to back out of.

steps.title: First in, first out
steps.text:
A **queue** gives back the item that has waited longest, like a line of people. The operations are **enqueue**, which adds at the back, and **dequeue**, which removes from the front.

An array can add at the back in one step with `push`. Removing from the front with `shift` is the trap: as the module on arrays showed, `shift` moves every remaining element, so it costs O(n). A queue that is emptied with `shift` costs O(n²) in total.

The fix is not to remove anything. Keep an index, `head`, that marks where the front of the queue is, and move the index forward. Reading the front and moving the index are both one step.

steps.text: Work from the prompt. A stack holds the numbers that are waiting for an operator.

steps.title: Build a queue
steps.text: Work from the prompt. Every operation must take one step, so do not call shift.

questions.prompt: What does the first line print?

choices.feedback: That is the order they went in. A stack gives back the newest first.
After c is popped, the newest remaining item is b.

`pop` returns the newest item each time: c, then b. Then d goes on top of a. `pop` on an empty array returns `undefined` and does not fail, so code that uses a stack has to decide what an empty stack means. In the bracket exercise it means a closing bracket with nothing to match.

questions.prompt: What does the second line print?

choices.feedback: Reading `queue[head++]` twice returns a and then b, the oldest first, and moves `head` to 2. The array still holds a and b, simply behind the head, never looked at again. The number waiting is the length minus `head`. The later module on graphs uses exactly this queue.
The array still holds four items, but the two behind head have already been taken.
Only a and b were taken. c is still waiting in front of d.
